title: Lists
subtitle: The Chalk Wall
martuIntro:
Seven numbers on my wall. I could give each one its own box. I could also lose my mind. A list keeps them together, in order, yes?
You have met lists already. `party.members` was one: the four of you, in order, under one name. Tonight we read a list closely, one position at a time.
goals: Make a [[list]] with square brackets and commas
Read an item by its [[index|position]], counting from 0, and from the end with `-1`
Change an item by its position, grow a list with `.append()`, and join two lists with `+`
Count items with `len()`, and know the last position is `len - 1`
Read a list inside a list, like `roster[3][1]`
Count with `range()`, cut a [[slice]] like `[-3:]`, and sort with `sorted()`

questions.explain: The call hands over 9, so inside the recipe `n` is 9. The recipe works out `9 * 2` and hands back 18. `print` shows what came back.
Python works out the right side first, with what's in the box now: 18 − 5 is 13. Then 13 goes back in the box, in place of the 18.

items.summary: Put the chalk wall's gaps in one list. Then read an item by its position, add to the list, count its items, and read a list inside a list.

exercises.title: How would you store it?
exercises.martu:
Store the seven gaps from my chalk wall in your code, any way you like. A *gap* is the hours between two bursts, the blasts from the leylines. Oldest first:
```text
48  48  47  46  44  41  37
```
In Unit 1 you kept one number in one box (a variable). Line 1, `hour_1 = 48`, keeps the first gap. It's done for you.
Try for two minutes, then press Run. There's no wrong try here, yes? If Python stops with an error, that's a try too. Read the box in the Console, then try one box per gap.

anotherWay.label: Seven boxes or one list
anotherWay.text:
```text
seven boxes:
 hour_1  hour_2  ...  hour_7
 [48]    [48]    ...  [37]

one list:
 chalk_wall
 [48, 48, 47, 46, 44, 41, 37]
```

anotherWay.label: Like a shopping list
anotherWay.text: You could write each thing to buy on its own scrap of paper. Or you could write one list, in order, on one page. Same things. One is easier to carry.
Any try is fine. Seven boxes work. The next exercise shows a shorter way.

exercises.title: Make the wall
exercises.martu:
A [[list]] keeps many values under one name, in order. In math class, a data set is a group of numbers you study together. A list is Python's data set: square brackets `[ ]` around it, and a comma between each two items. `marks = [46, 44, 41]` is a list of three items.
In math class, square brackets can group numbers, like parentheses. In Python they never group math. They make a list.
Numbers in a list get no quotes. Text keeps its quotes, like `["gold", "teal"]` in the Example.
```text
 chalk_wall = [48, 48, 47, ...]
             ^   ^   ^
          bracket  commas
```

anotherWay.label: A shelf of jars
anotherWay.text: Picture a shelf with seven jars in a row. The shelf has one name: `chalk_wall`. Each jar holds one gap. The order on the shelf is the order on the wall.

anotherWay.label: The wall as a list
anotherWay.text:
```text
chalk wall    48 48 47 46 44 41 37
               |  |  |  |  |  |  |
Python      [48,48,47,46,44,41,37]
```
Same numbers, same order. Brackets at the ends, commas in between.
I wrote each gap under the last, oldest at the top. Python reads a list left to right, oldest first. Same idea, turned on its side.

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text: In English, a series uses commas: 48, 48, 47 and 46. A Python list uses commas too, but no *and*, and it has square brackets at both ends: `[48, 48, 47, 46]`.
`[`, the gaps with commas between, `]`. No quotes.

exercises.title: The first is zero
exercises.martu:
Each item in a list has a position, its [[index]]. Positions count from 0, like a ruler: the first mark is 0, no steps from the start. So `chalk_wall[0]` is the oldest gap. A minus counts from the end: `chalk_wall[-1]` is the newest. The positions:
```text
 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
48 48 47 46 44 41 37
-7 -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1
```
As in English class, *seven* says how many and *seventh* says which one. The seventh gap is at position 6. There is no position 7, and no `-0`.
I test your code with other walls too, so read each gap by its position. Never type a number you see.
Try it if you like (it's not a step): add `print(chalk_wall[7])` and press Run. You'll see an [[IndexError]]. Then delete that line.

anotherWay.label: Jars numbered from 0
anotherWay.text:
```text
jar:  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
     [48][48][47][46][44][41][37]
```
The first jar's number is 0. Seven jars end at jar 6.

anotherWay.label: A ruler starts at 0
anotherWay.text: Look at a ruler. The first mark is 0, not 1. Position 0 means no steps from the start, and position 2 means two steps in: the third item.

```text
chalk_wall[0]   -> 48 (oldest)
chalk_wall[1]   -> 48
chalk_wall[6]   -> 37
chalk_wall[7]   -> IndexError
chalk_wall[-1]  -> 37 (newest)
chalk_wall[-2]  -> 41
```
Oogrish counts drills from the first stance, stance 0. Then one, two... He says the first one is only a warm-up. Python agrees with him.

exercises.martu:
[[append|`.append()`]] adds one item to the end of a list, the way an *appendix* goes at the end of a book. The dot speaks to the list: `chalk_wall.append(33)` means *chalk wall, add 33 to your end*. It changes the list itself.
`+` joins two lists into one new list, the way it glued text in Unit 1: `[41, 37] + [33]` makes `[41, 37, 33]`. The two old lists stay as they were.

exercises.title: How long is the wall?
exercises.martu:
[[len()|`len(wall)`]] counts the items in a list: `len(chalk_wall)` is 7. Positions start at 0, so the last position is one less, `len(wall) - 1`. It's *seven* and *seventh* again: 7 gaps, and the seventh is at position 6:
```text
len(wall)      ->  7
last position  ->  7 - 1 = 6
wall[6]        ->  37
```
A recipe (function) can take a whole list as its ingredient (parameter). Whatever list the call hands over, inside the recipe it's called `wall`. So `newest_mark(chalk_wall)` and `newest_mark([9, 8, 7])` both work.
Why the long way, when `[-1]` exists? In Unit 6, loops count from 0 to `len - 1`.

anotherWay.text:
```text
position: 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
          48 48 47 46 44 41 37
len = 7 items
last position = 7 - 1 = 6
```

Step 1, on the wall: `len(chalk_wall)` is 7, so `chalk_wall[len(chalk_wall) - 1]` is `chalk_wall[6]`, which is 37.
Step 2, in the recipe, for `newest_mark([9, 8, 7])`:
1. `wall` is `[9, 8, 7]`.
2. `len(wall)` is 3.
3. `len(wall) - 1` is 2.
4. `wall[2]` is 7. The recipe hands back 7.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work?
anotherWay.text: `len` counts from 1, but positions count from 0. So the count is always one past the last position. Take 1 away and you land on the last item, on a wall of any length.

exercises.title: Lists inside lists
exercises.martu:
A list can hold lists: a [[list inside a list]]. Read it like a theater ticket: row first, then seat. In `roster`, each row is a small list: a hero's name, then their mana (magic power). `roster[3]` is row 3, Lucky's. `roster[3][1]` reads row 3, then item 1 inside it:
```text
roster[3][1]
      |  |
      |  +-- item 1 of that row
      +----- row 3: ["Lucky", 26]
```
Rows and items both count from 0, so row 3 is the fourth row.

anotherWay.label: A table of rows
anotherWay.text:
```text
row  item 0         item 1
 0   "Oogrish"      18
 1   "Gearshift"    20
 2   "Bomb Shell"   24
 3   "Lucky"        26
```
Row first, then the item.

1. `roster[2]` is the row `["Bomb Shell", 24]`.
2. `[0]` of that row is `"Bomb Shell"`.

This code has three [[bug|bugs]], all loud: each one makes Python stop with an error. *Mend* means fix. Python shows one error at a time, so fix one, press Run again, and see what Python finds next. A new error is good news: Python got further.
When Python stops, read the box in the Console, in this order:
1. Read its title. It says what went wrong.
2. Read *Python's last line*. It says the same thing in Python's words.
3. Find the line number, and fix that line.

anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Python checks the grammar (the syntax) of every line before it runs any of them, so the comma bug on line 1 shows first.
2. Fix it and press Run again. A new error is good news: Python got further.
3. Fix line 2, then line 3, the same way.

exercises.title: Ranges
exercises.martu:
In math class, *range* means the biggest number minus the smallest. In Python, [[range()|`range(1, 7)`]] means something else: count from 1, and stop before 7. It's like a number line with a filled dot at 1 and an open dot at 7: 1 ≤ n < 7. `list(range(1, 7))` turns the count into a list, `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`:
```text
range(1, 7)
 1 2 3 4 5 6 | 7
             stop: left out
```
A *d8* is a die with 8 faces, numbered 1 to 8.

anotherWay.label: A ruler
anotherWay.text:
```text
range(1, 9)
|--|--|--|--|--|--|--|--|
1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9
^ start          stop ^
```
The stop mark is where you stop. You don't take it.

anotherWay.label: range or randint?
anotherWay.text: `random.randint(1, 8)` rolls ONE face, and 8 can come up. `list(range(1, 9))` lists EVERY face, and the 9 is left out. Different jobs, different ends.

1. Start at 1.
2. Count up by one.
3. Stop before the stop number.
4. `list(...)` collects them.
`range(start, stop)`: from the start, up to but not including the stop.

exercises.title: Slice the wall
exercises.martu:
A [[slice]] copies part of a list, like quoting a few lines of a poem in English class: you get an excerpt, and the poem doesn't change. `chalk_wall[2:5]` copies positions 2, 3 and 4. The end is left out, the same as `range`:
```text
 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
48 48 47 46 44 41 37
      [2:5] -> 47 46 44
```
In a book, "pages 2 to 5" includes page 5. A slice doesn't: it stops before its end number.
Leave a side empty to run to the edge. `chalk_wall[:3]` is the first three gaps. `chalk_wall[-2:]` is the last two.

anotherWay.label: Cut marks
anotherWay.text:
Cuts go BETWEEN the items:
```text
 | 48 | 48 | 47 | 46 |
 0    1    2    3    4
```
`[1:3]` cuts at 1 and at 3. What lies between: 48 and 47.

`chalk_wall[-3:]`:
1. Start 3 from the end: position -3, the 44.
2. No end number, so run to the edge.
3. You get `[44, 41, 37]`, a new list.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work?
anotherWay.text: A slice is a new list. Python copies the items out. Change `last_three` later, and `chalk_wall` stays the same. Change the wall, and the copy you made stays the same too.
`[start:stop]`: from the start, and stop before the stop. Leave a side empty to reach the edge.

exercises.title: `sorted` or `.sort`
exercises.martu:
[[sorted()|`sorted(chalk_wall)`]] hands back a sorted copy of the wall, smallest first. It's like photocopying a list and putting the copy in order: the original stays as it is. `shortest_first = sorted(chalk_wall)` keeps the copy.
`chalk_wall.sort()` puts the wall itself in order and hands back nothing. So `result = chalk_wall.sort()` puts `None` in `result`, Python's word for nothing. It's like a recipe with no `return` in Unit 3.

anotherWay.label: A copy or the original
anotherWay.text: `sorted()` is a friend who copies your list onto a new page, in order. `.sort()` rearranges your own page and hands you nothing back.

`result = chalk_wall.sort()`:
1. `.sort()` sorts `chalk_wall` itself.
2. It hands back nothing: `None`.
3. `result` gets that `None`.
`result = sorted(chalk_wall)`: `result` gets a new, sorted list.

anotherWay.label: A recipe with no return
anotherWay.text: In Unit 3, a recipe with no `return` handed back `None`. `.sort()` is like that: it does its job and hands back nothing. `sorted()` has a `return`, so to speak.

anotherWay.label: Not this
anotherWay.text:
Not this: `shortest_first = chalk_wall.sort()` (`None`: nothing came back). Not this: `shortest_first = chalk_wall` (the same list, a second name).
This: `shortest_first = sorted(chalk_wall)`.

exercises.title: How many times?
exercises.martu:
[[.count()]] counts how many times a value shows up in a list. It's a tally chart from math class: one tally mark for each match. `[7, 2, 7].count(7)` gives 2, because 7 shows up twice.
The dot works the way it did for `.append()`: it asks the list to do something. `bells.count(3)` means *bells, count your 3s*. The value goes inside the parentheses `( )`, and a number gets no quotes.
Oogrish ran a finger down my wall: *every forty-eight hours, at first.* On a long wall you'd lose count by eye, yes? Ask the list instead.

anotherWay.label: Tally marks
anotherWay.text:
```text
wall:  48 48 47 46 44 41 37
48?    ✓  ✓  .  .  .  .  .
```
`.count(48)` makes one tally mark for each 48, like a tally chart in math class. Two marks, so it gives 2.

anotherWay.label: Counting socks
anotherWay.text: How many red socks are in the drawer? You don't count every sock, only the red ones. `len(drawer)` counts every sock. `drawer.count("red")` counts only the red ones.

`chalk_wall.count(48)`:
1. Python takes the list `chalk_wall`.
2. It checks each item in order: is it the same as 48?
3. It hands back how many said yes: 2.
`wall.count(48)`: how many items are 48. Parentheses, and no quotes on numbers.

items.title: Oogrish's Training Log
items.summary: Keep Oogrish's training log as a list of pairs. Add a drill, fix a score, and write a recipe that hands back the newest score.
items.intro:
Oogrish trains every morning and gives each drill a score. A *drill* is one practice move, like a cane parry. He wants a *log*: a list that keeps every drill and its score.
Each drill is a pair, a small list: `["kick", 3]` is the drill, then its score. The log is a list of pairs: a [[list inside a list]], like the roster in Many Values, One Name.
Do the six tasks in order. Each one has a note in your code, from `# 1.` to `# 6.` Use any drills you like.
items.martu:
Read a list inside a list one step at a time, like a theater ticket: the row first, then the seat. `log[0]` is the first pair. `log[0][1]` is position 1 inside that pair: its score.
I test your code with other logs, full of made-up drills. So read every drill and score from the list, by its position. Never type a score you can see.
Task 4 is a recipe (function), as in Unit 3. Its ingredient is `training`: inside the recipe, that's the name for whatever log the call hands over.

anotherWay.label: A list of pairs, drawn out
anotherWay.text:
```text
log[0] -> ["cane parry", 7]
log[1] -> ["shield wall", 5]
log[2] -> ["slow breaths", 9]

log[0][0] -> "cane parry"
log[0][1] -> 7
```
The first number picks the pair. The second number picks the part inside it: 0 for the drill, 1 for the score.

anotherWay.label: A score card
anotherWay.text: A score card has one row per drill: the drill's name, then its score. The log is the card, and each pair is a row. `log[0][1]` is the first row (position 0), score column (position 1).

1. Put 3 or more pairs inside `log = []`.
2. Add one more pair with `log.append([...])`.
3. Change the first score: `log[0][1] = log[0][1] + 2`.
4. In the recipe, hand back `training[-1][1]`.
5. Glue the drill from `log[-1]` to `str(last_score(log))`, and print it.
6. Print `len(log)`.

exercises.title: Insert and pop
exercises.martu:
[[.insert()]] puts a new item into a list at a position: the position first, then the value. Every item after it moves back one place, like a lunch line when a friend steps in. If `marks` is `[5, 7]`, `marks.insert(1, 6)` makes it `[5, 6, 7]`. `.append()` always adds at the end. `.insert()` can add anywhere.
[[.pop()]] does the opposite: it takes the last item off the list and hands it back, so you can keep it in a variable. `last = marks.pop()` takes the 7 off and keeps it in `last`.
Lucky leaned on my wall, and one mark rubbed off: the 47. Put it back, with no retyping.

anotherWay.label: Squeezing in
anotherWay.text:
```text
before:   48 48 46 44 41 37
position:  0  1  2  3  4  5

.insert(2, 47)
after:    48 48 47 46 44 41 37
```
46 and every gap after it moved back one place.

anotherWay.label: A lunch line
anotherWay.text: A friend steps into the lunch line at position 2: everyone behind them moves back one place. That's `.insert()`. The last person in line walks off, and you write down who it was. That's `.pop()`.

1. `chalk_wall.insert(2, 47)`: 47 goes in at position 2.
2. `newest = chalk_wall.pop()`: the last gap comes off, into `newest`.
3. Press Run, and look at both lines in the Console.
`.insert(position, value)` adds. `.pop()` takes the last off and hands it back.

exercises.title: Biggest and smallest
exercises.martu:
[[max() and min()|max()]] hands back the biggest number in a list, and `min()` hands back the smallest, wherever they are. In math class, that's the maximum and the minimum of a data set: same words, same idea. `max([41, 46, 39])` is 46.
[[sum()]] adds up every number in the list: `sum([5, 10])` is 15.
The list goes inside the parentheses, the way it does in `len(chalk_wall)`. There's no dot in front.
Gearshift asks three questions every night. Which gap was longest? Which was shortest? How many hours in all?

anotherWay.label: Measuring the class
anotherWay.text: Who is tallest? Who is shortest? Measure everyone, then pick: that's `max()` and `min()`. How many minutes did the whole class read this week? Add everyone's minutes: that's `sum()`.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math class, the biggest number minus the smallest is the *range* of a data set. Step 3 works out the wall's range: `longest - shortest`. Python's `range()` is something else: it counts, like `range(1, 7)`.

1. `max(chalk_wall)` looks at every gap and hands back the biggest.
2. `min(chalk_wall)` hands back the smallest.
3. `sum(chalk_wall)` adds them all.
4. `longest - shortest` is the shrink.
`max(wall)` is the biggest, `min(wall)` the smallest, and `sum(wall)` all of them added up.

items.title: Quiz: Ranges, Slices and Sorting
items.summary: Optional quiz: 8 questions on `range()`, slices, and `sorted()` versus `.sort()`. Retake it as often as you like.

questions.explain: `range(3, 7)` starts at 3 and stops *before* 7, like a number line with an open dot at 7. So 7 is left out: 3, 4, 5, 6.

questions.q: A d10 is a die with 10 faces, numbered 1 to 10. Which `range` gives exactly those 10 numbers?

whyWrong.0: `range` stops before its end number, so `range(1, 10)` stops at 9.
whyWrong.1: `range(10)` starts at 0 and stops at 9, and a d10 has no 0 face.
whyWrong.2: This starts at 0, and a d10 has no 0 face. It also stops at 9.

questions.explain: `range(1, 11)` gives 1 up to 10, because it stops before 11. `randint(1, 10)`, from Unit 2, is different: it includes both ends.
`.sort()` sorts `wall` itself and hands back nothing, which Python calls `None`. So `x` holds `None`, like the answer from a recipe with no `return`.

questions.q: This program should print the gaps shortest first, but it prints `None`. Fix it.
questions.explain: `sorted(wall)` hands back a sorted copy, so `ordered` holds it. `wall.sort()` hands back `None`.
Position 1 is the second 48. A slice stops *before* its end number, so it takes positions 1 and 2: `[48, 47]`.

questions.q: Fill the blank so the program prints the two newest gaps. Count from the end, so it works for a wall of any length.
questions.explain: `[-2:]` starts two from the end and runs to the very end, so it works for a wall of any length. `[2:]` also prints `[41, 37]` here, but only because this wall has four gaps.

questions.q: Put the lines in order so the program prints the three newest gaps in `wall`, shortest first.
questions.explain: Slice first, then sort a copy with `sorted()`. `.sort()` would hand back `None`, and `[-3:-1]` leaves out the newest gap.
The call hands over `[9, 8, 7]`, so inside the recipe `wall` holds it. The recipe hands back `wall[:2]`: from the start, stopping before position 2. That is `[9, 8]`.

items.title: Tuples: Pairs That Can't Change
items.summary: A tuple is like a list that can't change, written with parentheses: `(12, 5)`. Read it by position, or give each item its own name.
items.body:
Some values come in pairs that always go together. In math class, a point on a graph is a pair like (3, 8): across first, then up. The order matters, and both numbers belong to the same point. A spot on the map of Tor works the same way: 12 across, 5 down.
For pairs like these, Python has the [[tuple]]. It is like a list, but it uses parentheses `( )` instead of square brackets `[ ]`:
```python
spot = (12, 5)
```
You read a tuple the same way you read a list. `spot[0]` is 12, `spot[-1]` is 5, and `len(spot)` is 2.
But a tuple can't change. `spot[0] = 3` makes Python stop with a [[TypeError]] that says a tuple *does not support item assignment*: you can't put a new item in. A tuple has no `.append()` either.
Why use a list you can't change? A tuple says: these values belong together, in this order. Nobody changes one by mistake.
Check which marks you typed. `[48, 47]` is a list. `(48, 47)` is a tuple. If Python says a tuple *has no attribute 'append'*, you typed parentheses where square brackets belong. Here, parentheses make a tuple. They don't group math, the way they do in PEMDAS.
One more trick: *unpacking*. It gives each item its own name, in one line. Put two names on the left of `=`, and they get the items in order:
```python
name, mana = ("Lucky", 26)
```
Now `name` holds `"Lucky"` and `mana` holds 26. It's like math class saying: if (x, y) is (3, 8), then x is 3 and y is 8.

exercises.title: A spot on the map
exercises.martu:
A [[tuple]] is a few values that stay together, in order, and can't change. In math class, a point on a graph is a pair like (3, 8): across first, then up. A tuple is that kind of pair. It uses parentheses `( )`, not square brackets: `door = (3, 8)`.
*Unpacking* gives each item its own name, in one line. `row, seat = door` puts 3 in `row` and 8 in `seat`. Math class says it this way: if (x, y) is (3, 8), then x is 3 and y is 8.
Here the parentheses make a tuple. They don't group math, the way they do in PEMDAS. My cabin sits at 12 across, 5 down on the map of Tor, and the cabin does not move, yes?

anotherWay.label: Two seats, bolted down
anotherWay.text:
```text
cabin = (12, 5)
         |   |
    across   down
```
A tuple is like a row of seats bolted to the floor. You can read who sits in each seat, but you can't add a seat or take one away.

anotherWay.label: A street address
anotherWay.text: A street address is a house number, then a street name. It always has both, always in that order, and it doesn't change when you visit. A tuple works the same way.

1. `cabin = (12, 5)`: parentheses, with a comma between the numbers.
2. `across, down = cabin`: `across` gets item 0, and `down` gets item 1.
3. `print(across, down)` shows `12 5`.
`( )` makes a tuple, which can't change. `row, seat = door` unpacks it, in order.

items.title: zip(): Two Lists, Side by Side
items.summary: Pair up two lists that line up, item by item, with `zip()`: first with first, second with second.
items.body:
Sometimes two lists go together, item by item:
```python
heroes = ["Oogrish", "Lucky"]
manas = [18, 26]
```
`heroes[0]` goes with `manas[0]`, and `heroes[1]` goes with `manas[1]`. It's like a table in math class with two columns: each row pairs a name with a number. Two lists that line up like this are called [[parallel lists]].
[[zip()]] pairs them up. It works like the zipper on a coat, which joins the two sides tooth by tooth: first with first, second with second. Each pair is a [[tuple]], a pair in parentheses.
```python
pairs = list(zip(heroes, manas))
```
Now `pairs` holds `[('Oogrish', 18), ('Lucky', 26)]`.
Why the `list()`? On its own, `zip()` hands back a zipper nobody has pulled yet. If you print it, you see something like `<zip object at 0x7f3a...>`. `list()` pulls the zipper, so you can see the pairs. You did the same with `list(range(1, 7))`.
If one list is shorter, `zip()` stops when the shorter list runs out. There is no error: the extra items are left out.
You've seen this in the campaign. Mar'tu's four replies sat in four boxes, `option_1` to `option_4`, and the game matched `"option 1"` to the first one. Two lists and a `zip()` can do that matching.

exercises.title: Spell colors
exercises.martu:
[[zip()]] pairs up two lists, item by item, like the zipper on a coat: the first tooth on one side meets the first tooth on the other. Each pair is a tuple. Put `zip()` inside `list()` to see the pairs, the way you did with `list(range(1, 7))`: `list(zip(coins, values))` gives `[('copper', 1), ('brass', 5)]`.
Every hero's magic has a color. Oogrish's is gold, and Gearshift's is fire orange. Your `heroes` and `colors` lists are in the same order, so the first hero goes with the first color, yes?

`zip()` joins the two sides tooth by tooth: the first with the first, the second with the second.

items.title: The Basement Inventory
items.summary: Track the parts in Mar'tu's basement with two lists that line up. Insert, pop, sort a copy, count and zip.
items.intro:
You'll build two lists that line up, called [[parallel lists]]: `parts` holds the names of the parts, and `counts` holds how many of each part there are. `counts[0]` goes with `parts[0]`, like the two columns of a table in math class. Whatever you do to one list, do the same to the other.
Under the trap door, Mar'tu's basement is full of brass parts for the resonance array, his machine of brass instruments. Bomb Shell keeps the inventory: a list of what is down there, and how many.
There are seven tasks, in order. In your code, the notes `# 1.` to `# 7.` mark where each one goes. Pick any parts you like. Can't decide? Press the Mar'tu's pick button, next to Names to use.
Before this, do the lesson More List Tools (`.insert()` and `.pop()`), How many times? in Extra practice (`.count()`), and the zip() article.
items.martu:
Two lists, one inventory. Keep them lined up: when you add or take away an item in `parts`, do the same in `counts`. If they get out of line, the lens gets the coil's count, and my array lies to me, yes?
I test your code with other lists, with other parts. So read every number from the lists, the way a formula in math class works for any numbers. Don't type in a number you can see.

parts  lens   fork   coil

Position 0 on one shelf goes with position 0 on the other. If you insert on one shelf, insert on the other too.

anotherWay.label: A shopping list with amounts
anotherWay.text: A list of things to buy, and next to it how many of each. Cross out the eggs, and you must cross out the 12 too. Otherwise the milk gets the eggs' number.

1. `parts = [...]` and `counts = [...]`, the same length.
2. `.insert(1, ...)` into both.
3. `borrowed = parts.pop()`, then `counts.pop()`.
4. `sorted(counts)[-3:]`: a copy, so `counts` stays lined up.
5. `counts.count(0)`.
6. `list(zip(parts, counts))`.

campaignLink.why: Bomb Shell and Lucky spent two weeks in this basement, hunched over Mar'tu's brass instruments. This time you keep the list of what is down there.

items.takeaway: Parallel lists: whatever you do to one, do to the other. `.insert(1, ...)` puts an item second, `.pop()` takes the last, `sorted()` makes a copy, and `zip()` pairs them.

items.title: One List, Same Answer
items.summary: A stretch: rewrite a program that uses seven boxes so it uses one list. It shows the same three lines, and works out the shrink from the list.
items.martu:
Rewriting code to do the same job in a better way is like revising an essay in English class. The ideas stay the same, but the sentences get clearer. Before you knew lists, my wall lived in seven boxes, `hour_1` to `hour_7`. Rewrite the program with one list, `chalk_wall`. Show the same three lines, word for word.
The old program has a typed-in answer: `print("Shrink:", 11)`. The *shrink* is how much the gap got shorter, the oldest gap minus the newest. Let the code work it out from the list. I test your code with another wall, so read every number from the list, yes?

anotherWay.label: Seven boxes, one list
anotherWay.text:
```text
hour_1 ... hour_7
  48  ...   37

chalk_wall[0] ... [-1]
  48   ...   37
```
`hour_1` becomes `chalk_wall[0]`. `hour_7` becomes `chalk_wall[-1]`, the newest on a wall of any length.

1. Put the seven numbers in `chalk_wall`, oldest first.
2. Delete the seven `hour_` lines.
3. Each `print` reads from the list: the oldest at `[0]`, the newest at `[-1]`.
4. The shrink is the oldest minus the newest, worked out from those two reads.

anotherWay.label: One page, not seven scraps
anotherWay.text: Seven scraps of paper, one number each, and the total written on a scrap by hand. Add a scrap, and the total is wrong. Write the numbers on one page, and work the total out from the page.

campaignLink.why: You have seen this wall. Oogrish ran a finger down it, and the newest number, 37, was circled twice. One list holds the whole wall. When a new gap is chalked, every read and the shrink change to match when you press Run again.

items.takeaway: One list in place of seven boxes: `[0]` is the oldest, `[-1]` the newest, and the code works out the shrink, so it changes to match a new wall.
items.pairTalk: Pair talk: before you start, tell your partner which box holds the oldest gap and which holds the newest, and which position of a list reads each one.

exercises.title: Make, append, fix, read
exercises.martu:
Lucky copied three marks for you. Four steps: make the list, append your guess, fix Lucky's mistake by its position, and print the last item. I test your code with another list, so read every number from the list. Don't type in a number you can see.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Many Values, One Name. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

items.title: Quick Check 4 · Form A questions
items.summary: Two questions that go with Quick Check 4. To pass the Quick Check, get both right.

questions.q: `chalk_wall` holds `[48, 48, 47, 46, 44, 41, 37]`. `roster` holds four rows: `["Oogrish", 18]`, `["Gearshift", 20]`, `["Bomb Shell", 24]` and `["Lucky", 26]`. What will these three lines print?
questions.explain: `[-2]` is second from the end: 41. `len` counts the gaps: 7, while the last position is 6. Row 1 is the second row, because rows start at 0, and `[0]` is its name: Gearshift.
`range(1, 4)` counts 1, 2, 3 and stops before 4, like the open dot on a number line. `+` joins two lists into one, so 9 goes at the end as an item of its own, not inside its own square brackets.

exercises.title: Make, append, fix, read
exercises.martu:
Bomb Shell's Velocite ore powers everything. `ore_used` is how many chunks of ore he used each day, oldest day first. Lucky copied three of the days for you. Four steps: make the list, append your guess, fix Lucky's mistake by its position, and print the last item. I test your code with another list, so read every number from the list. Don't type in a number you can see.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to the lesson Many Values, One Name. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

items.summary: Two questions that go with Quick Check 4. To pass the Quick Check, get both right.

questions.q: `ore_used` holds `[2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7]`. `drills` holds four rows: `["cane parry", 7]`, `["shield wall", 5]`, `["slow breaths", 9]` and `["roll and rise", 6]`. What will these three lines print?
questions.explain: `[-2]` is second from the end: 5. `len` counts the days: 6, while the last position is 5. Row 1 is the second row, because rows start at 0, and `[0]` is its name: shield wall.
`range(2, 5)` counts 2, 3, 4 and stops before 5, like the open dot on a number line. `+` joins two lists into one, so 8 goes at the end as an item of its own, not inside its own square brackets.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Lists
items.summary: All of Unit 4 on one page, ready to print.

entries.note: Square brackets go around the items, and a comma goes between each two. Numbers get no quotes. (Lesson: Many Values, One Name)
Positions start at 0, like a ruler. `[1]` is the second item.
A minus counts from the end. `[-1]` is the last item of a list of any length.
Fix one item by its position. The rest of the list stays as it is.
Adds one item to the end of the list itself, like an appendix at the end of a book.
`+` joins two lists into a new one. `wall + 33` stops with a TypeError: `+` needs a list on both sides.
`len()` counts the items. The last position is one less, `len - 1`, here 2, because positions start at 0.

entries.concept: A recipe that takes a list
entries.note: Use the ingredient `wall`, so it works for any list it is handed. `wall[-1]` is the short way. (Lesson: Many Values, One Name)
Read it like a theater ticket: row first, then seat. `roster[3]` is row 3, and `[1]` is item 1 in that row.
It counts 1 to 6: the stop is left out, like the open dot on a number line. `list()` turns the count into a list. (Lesson: Reading the Wall Closely)
A slice copies part of a list, like quoting a few lines of a poem. The end is left out: `[0:2]` copies positions 0 and 1. With no end number, it runs to the end of the list.
`sorted()` hands back a sorted copy and leaves `wall` alone. `.sort()` sorts `wall` itself and hands back `None`: nothing comes back.
IndexError: list index out of range means there is no item at that position. Three items sit at positions 0, 1 and 2. For the last item, use `[-1]`, never `[len(wall)]`.
TypeError: 'list' object is not callable means Python tried to run the list like a recipe. Read a list with square brackets: `wall[0]`.
SyntaxError: invalid syntax means Python can't read the line, like a sentence with broken grammar. Perhaps you forgot a comma? Inside a list, a comma goes between each two items.
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable means you used `[ ]` on `None`. `x` holds `None`, because nothing came back. Use `sorted(wall)`.
Counts how many items are 48. `len()` counts every item. (Extra practice: Reading the Wall)
`.insert(position, value)` squeezes an item in. `.pop()` takes the last item off and hands it back. (Lesson: More List Tools)
`.remove()` takes a value, not a position. `in` asks: is it there?
The biggest, the smallest, and the total, wherever they sit.
Like a list that can't change, written with parentheses. Two names on the left of `=` unpack it: each name gets one item, in order. (Article: Tuples)
Pairs two lists, first with first, second with second. Put it inside `list()` to see the pairs. (Article: zip())
